content: Tuberculous pericarditis was first identified by Rokitansky, an English scientist, in 1852. It occurs due to the hematogenous or lymphatic spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the pericardium. This leads to acute inflammation of the pericardium, with infiltration of polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs) and leukocytes. The condition can result in pericardial effusion and fibrinous changes in the pericardium. The visceral pericardium thickens due to fibrin deposition, which can progress to constrictive pericarditis. There are four pathological stages of tuberculous pericarditis: 1. Stage 1 involves diffuse fibrin deposition, granulomas, and abundant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. 2. Stage 2 is characterized by serous or serosanguineous pericardial effusion, predominantly lymphocytic exudate, and the presence of monocytes and foam cells. 3. Stage 3 includes absorption of the effusion, granulomatous caseation, and pericardial thickening due to fibrin and collagen deposition. 4. Stage 4 involves the development of constrictive pericarditis, with obliteration of the pericardial space by dense adhesions, marked thickening of the parietal layer, and replacement of granulomas with fibrous tissue. Conditions associated with tuberculous pericarditis include pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), HIV infection, malignancy, chemotherapy, and diabetes mellitus. Gross pathological findings include a thickened pericardium, shaggy hemorrhage, and exudate. Microscopic analysis often reveals acid-fast bacilli, which are characteristic of the disease. The prevalence of tuberculous pericarditis is approximately 1–2% among patients with pulmonary tuberculosis. It can affect individuals of all age groups, but its incidence increases with age and is more common in elderly individuals. It predominantly affects individuals of Black race and is more frequent in men than women. The disease is most commonly reported in regions with high TB prevalence, such as South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, India, and China. Patients with tuberculous pericarditis often have a history of pulmonary TB, HIV infection, immune dysfunction, or exposure to TB-endemic areas. Common symptoms include fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, breathlessness, chest pain, malaise, and ankle edema. On physical examination, patients may appear cachectic and present with fever, tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, hypotension, tachypnea, jugular venous pressure (JVP) distension, Kussmaul's sign, lymphadenopathy, pleural dullness, decreased breath sounds, pericardial rub, pericardial knock, hepatomegaly, ascites, distant heart sounds, and signs of cardiomegaly. Laboratory findings may include mild anemia, normal leukocyte count, exudative pericardial effusion, and the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacilli in pericardial fluid. A positive HIV test may also be observed. Diagnostic imaging, such as ECG, chest X-ray, echocardiography, CT scan, and MRI, can provide valuable insights. ECG findings may include low-voltage QRS complexes, inverted T waves, atrial fibrillation, and electrical alternans. Chest X-rays may show pericardial calcification, thickening, effusion, or evidence of pulmonary TB. Echocardiography and ultrasound can reveal pericardial effusion, thickening, and abnormal ventricular dimensions. CT and MRI findings may include pericardial calcification, thickening, effusion, and lymphadenopathy. Pericardiocentesis is the gold standard diagnostic test for tuberculous pericarditis. Acid-fast bacilli in pericardial fluid confirm the diagnosis. If acid-fast bacilli are not detected in sputum or pericardial fluid, a pericardial biopsy may be necessary. Treatment involves a 2-month course of isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin, and ethambutol, followed by a 4-month course of isoniazid and rifampicin. Short-course chemotherapy is particularly beneficial for HIV-infected patients. Medical therapy is the mainstay of treatment, while pericardiectomy is reserved for patients with resistant constrictive pericarditis. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of tuberculous pericarditis.
